Hi Sarah / Tom —

Thanks again for the call today — really useful context. Quick recap and proposed next steps to keep momentum: 

Top takeaways:
- Primary use case: low-latency customer support assistant (streaming replies) + nightly batch reranking/embeddings for search.
- P95 latency target: <= 300ms for single-turn web chat; throughput for batch rerank ~20k docs/night.
- Key concerns: feature parity with hyperscaler APIs (function/tool calling, structured outputs), vendor lock-in, and cost predictability.

Proposed next steps:
1) Redwoods vs hyperscalers one-pager (attached) — quick differentiators.
2) Technical perf + feature tests: SE-led benchmarks on streaming, function/tool-calling compatibility, and structured output (JSON schema enforcement).
3) Pilot scope: 2-week sandbox with a sample chat flow + batch rerank job. We can provide test harness and suggestions for metrics.

Would you be open to scheduling the baseline perf run next Tuesday? If yes, can you share a small sample dataset (anonymized) and a test user account or API endpoint for the rerank job?

Attachments: redwood_vs_hyperscalers_one-pager.pdf, acme-proposed-test-plan.xlsx

Subject: Re: Follow-up: Competitive eval & feature-parity tests

Hi Sarah —

I can take the technical lead on the feature-parity and perf tests. Quick answers up front and then a proposed minimal test plan.

Short answers — high level:
- Function/tool calling: Redwood supports structured tool calling and verified function invocation similar to hyperscalers, but with a couple of differences: we expose a richer tool-routing policy (route to private connectors or hosted connectors), and our validation layer can run deterministic schema checks before/after invocation. We also provide SDK helper hooks for retries and idempotency.
- Structured outputs: We support strict JSON schema enforcement and granular failure modes (partial/invalid payloads flagged separately). For dev workflows, we provide a structured-output validation step in the SDK and a toggle to reject vs sanitize invalid responses.
- Streaming: Our runtime supports chunked token streaming with partial function call streaming (you can receive arguments progressively and begin execution), plus explicit end-of-stream markers to avoid ambiguity. Latency tradeoffs are configurable (e.g., aggressive batching vs strict per-request latency).

Proposed minimal test plan (attached is a more detailed spreadsheet):
1) Feature parity checks (1 day) — call a standard function set (3 sample tools): fetch_user_profile, lookup_inventory, send_email. Verify call/response schemas and retry behavior.
2) Streaming correctness (1 day) — run 200 concurrent short chat sessions, inspect partial function arg arrival and final payloads. Metrics: first-byte latency, function-arg latency, error rate.
3) Perf baseline (2 days) — run single-turn generation at various tokens/seq-lens and measure p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1k tokens. Repeat against your AWS endpoint using same prompts to compare.
4) Rerank batch (1 day) — submit your sample dataset (anonymized). Measure throughput (docs/hour), memory footprint, and cost estimate.

What we need from you:
- Short-term API key (scoped) or allowlisted IP range + target dataset sample (~1k docs).
- A set of 8 representative prompts and 3 function/tool definitions we should test.

I'll prep a skeleton test harness and share a link to the results dashboard. If acceptable, Marissa and I can schedule the runs starting next Tuesday.

- Rishi
